They then brought them back to Dhankawadi around 11 pm, allegedly robbed them of more money and left with threats of murder if they went to the police.

On Saturday, the rapists called up the Dhankawadi woman and demanded Rs 10,000. This time, she informed the Sahkarnagar police, who set a trap and arrested the men in the process of accepting money.

The accused have been remanded to police custody till September 12. Police inspector Shailendra Shinde is investigating the case.

Heading: Vintage beauties turn heads on city roads - Indian Express
Content:
Mummy, don't commit a sin...
You should show some courage...
I will stand on my feet...
I also dream of taking saat pheras...
The mehendi will dazzle on my hands...

The plea comes from an unborn girl child; her words are scripted on a six-foot-tall board next to the Ganesh pandal of the Sangharsh Mitra Mandal, Sambhajinagar (Chinchwad).

The Sangarsh mandal has taken up female foeticide as its theme while decorating its pandal. Across the pandal are messages urging parents not to kill the unborn child if it happens to be a girl. Families are warned that sex determination tests are an offence entailing three to five years jail term and a fine.

The decorations have cast a spell on the crowd in the twin industrial town of Pimpri-Chinchwad. And the most impressed seems to be the medical department of the Pimpri-Chinchwad Municipal Corporation (PCMC), which has decided to put up a miniature version of the decoration in eight civic-run hospitals and 13 dispensaries.

"The Sangharsh mandal has done a wonderful job. Such an effort to spread awareness about female foeticide is the need of the hour," says PCMC medical director Rajshekhar Iyer. He said the medical department has told the mandal volunteers to hand over small colour prints of the decoration so that they can be put up in every hospital and dispensary run by the civic body.

Civic activists say if the medical department keeps its word, it would probably be the first time in Pune that a Ganesh decoration has found such acceptability and put to greater use for public awareness. "Normally, decorations are forgettable. Very few mandals show imagination or creativity in putting up decorations. A handful of mandals do make an effort to pass on messages highlighting public issues, but they lack impact," says activist Shridhar Chalkha, who, too, has words of praise for the decoration of Sangharsh mandal.

"We are trying to make a point that the increasing urge among parents for a male child will ultimate cause an imbalance in society. This is dangerous for peace in a civilised society," says 26-year-old Shakib Khan.

"This decoration has not been put up just for the sake of it. The crowd comes to have a quick look but then stands rooted to the ground... reading the messages and listening to the narration on the loudspeakers," says a proud Khan, founder of the mandal.

Delighted at the PCMC honour for the decoration, Khan hopes that from next year many mandals will follow suit and help increase awareness on public issues.

The Sangharsh mandal comprises about 40 youngsters, all but four of them undergraduates, aged between of 22 to 27. Several of them are industrial workers earning Rs 5,000 to Rs 6,000 per month. "There was unanimity among us about putting up decorations on female foeticide. All of us feel strongly about the issue," says Khan.

Heading: Diego Rivera wins in record time - Indian Express
Content:
The classic cars at the Pune Festival 2008 - Car Fiesta were flagged off on Sunday at 11 am from the Centre for Police Research, Pashan by Major General Noble Thamburaj.

The first to leave the stable was the Wolseley Landaulet 1908, owned by Abbas Jasdanwalla. It was the oldest car in the rally. There were 54 beauties in all. Prominent among them were the Mercedes Benz 230 SL 1966 belonging to Fali Dhondy and both, the Mercedes Benz C-200 2008 and the Hummer H-3 2008, owned by Subhash Sanas. Yohan Poonawalla also showcased his Bentley Flying Spur 2007 and Rolls Royce Phantom 2005.

An enthusiastic crowd turned up on Sunday morning to greet the participants. Aditya Bharitiya's Dodge Charger 1972 seemed to attract a lot of attention. Poonawalla's Jaguar E-type 1975 was another favourite of the crowd. Red in colour and stunning to look at, it used to be an icon of the 1960's motoring. The aggressive slatted grill and flared wheel arches were eye-catching and raised a collective gasp among the audience.

The route of the rally was marked from the Centre for Police Research, on to Pashan road, past the NCL-ARDE gate, to Chandni Chowk and finally to the NDA gate before taking a U turn and returning on the same route to the starting point.

Heading: Compensation sought - Indian Express
Content:
The city police on Sunday claimed that all the allegations of rape by the 17-year-old Hyderabad based minor girl were false.

The girl, who was rescued from the red light area in Budhwar Peth in 2006, had alleged that 14 personnel from the Pune city police raped her at a lodge in Nana Peth in February 2005. Divisional assistant commissioner of police Suresh Pote told the media persons that girl was clearly lying.

"She had made similar allegation against the Hyderbad police last year. The Hyderbad police in four offences wanted her advocate named Khalid, who has now gone absconding," said Pote. "We don't know the intention of the girl. But she has made false allegations damaging the reputation of Pune police," he added. Pote admitted that a team of Hyderabad police has rescued the girl from the brothel in Budhwar Peth in January 2006.

The girl had also said that Faraskhana police had arrested her on the day of Dashehra in 2005. She alleged that police noted her name as "Seema" from Nimbada in Rajashthan despite of telling them repeatedly that she was from Hyderbad.

When asked, Pote said "Seema" was her assumed name. While the city police claimed her allegations as baseless, the girl maintained that whatever she said was truth.

The girl told the media persons that a high profile person, who raped her in Hyderabad, influenced the police to file false complaints against her lawyer Khalid. Meanwhile, the crime branch has initiated a probe into this matter.

Heading: Not Kidding - Indian Express
Content:
Teacher's Day
For Bhawna Balsaver, it was a journey back to her school days on her new show on Star One, Paani Puri. Balsaver is portraying a character called Veena Paani and what is weird is that she had a teacher in school who was also called Veena Paani. And the coincidences don't end there. Apparently, just like her old teacher, Balsaver's character is also obsessive about cleanliness. Talk about a blast from the past.

Career switch
The coincidences never end in the world of television. Aastha Chaudhary, the lead actress on Babul ka Aangann Chootey Na, is an engineer by qualification. So is the latest entrant on the show—model-turned-actor Abhinav Shukla. The actor, who plays Aastha's college buddy Ratan in a month-long cameo, too possesses an engineer degree. Shukla's run on the show may get extended. The 24-year old has an impressive portfolio from his modeling days— he's modeled for high-profile brands like TagHeuer, Peter England and Van Heusen..

Long lost love?
Another new entrant on another popular show is Faisal Raza on Kumkum. Raza will be playing the role of Sarjan Singh, a Jat, who is Kumkum's father's friend. Sarjan's marriage had been arranged with Kumkum, when they were both children and he returns years later to claim her. Kumkum on her part has to continue pretending to be Sumeet's wife, so as to avoid the uncouth Sarjan. A complicated set of circumstances, indeed.

Heading: Cn & Heard - Indian Express
Content:
Being a child artiste is not child's play anymore. It takes much more than being chubby and cute

In the early years of television in India, a certain chubby-faced Master Bittu was cast to add that cutesy element to shows. Or a pretty-looking Baby Guddi who viewers could adore. Few episodes into the serial, their role was restricted to a bare minimum or they grew up to be the main protagonist. But in recent times, the responsibilities of child artistes have increased manifold. "They are the backbone of our script and they can carry the entire serial on their tender shoulders," says Arun Mavnoor, director of Main Teri Parchayi Hoon on NDTV Imagine, a serial which narrates the plight of three children after the death of their mother.

Megha Gupta who plays Aanchal in the same show has a similar view but she feels this sudden transition towards performance-oriented roles for children is because of advancement of television in India. "Today, directors want to capture all kinds of emotions and they want character to be uniquely different from each other," says Gupta.

While children these days are required to laugh, cry and fight in serials, Colors' show Balika Vadhu deals with a more mature topic, that of child marriage. "While there have been roles written for children of late, this is the first serial that actually has children playing lead roles and addressing the age-old problem of child marriage," says Sunjoy Wadhwa, producer of Balika Vadhu. Wadhwa also praises the maturity and dedication these tiny tots exhibit. "You don't have to repeat the scene to them. They listen very attentively to you and grasp every detail. In fact it is easier working with them."

Mavnoor talks about the special needs one has to bear in mind before having children as part of their cast. "When you have really young kids, playing major roles, one must make sure that they are provided food on time. Adequate rest and sleep are also a must."

But these young guns are not main protagonists for nothing. They work as hard as the adults in the unit. Nine-year-old Aditansh, who plays the role of Ayush in Main Teri puts in 12 to 14 hours of shooting per day. "It is very difficult to manage shooting and school. But I make sure I study whenever I get the time," he says, adding, "Initially it was tough mouthing dialogues, but all the senior actors were very supportive and helped me out."

If you thought performances are restricted to just soaps, then you must watch Amey Pandya and Swini Khare perform on the reality dance show Zara Nachke Dikha. "They are more talented than the older members of the team. Their raw energy and enthusiasm just makes you feel that there is more competition than ever before," says Ali Asgar, the captain of the boys' team on the show.

Having children on a show also lightens the atmosphere on the sets. "Playing with them and listening to their stories could have you rolling on the floor with laughter," says Gupta. Wadhwa agrees, "But at times when they are unwell, it does take a toll on the entire unit."

Heading: Indiabulls guilty of causing mental agony - Indian Express
Content:
Night out!
"Don't worry we will go to the Timber Trail this evening Sanjeev. We will just complete the bail arguments and you will be out", smiled a senior advocate, defence counsel for Sanjeev Bansal, co- accused in Judge-Bribery case. Much to Sanjeev's chagrin, the Court refused to hear the arguments and the public prosecutor refused to argue the bail petition on Saturday.

Long time! We missed You
Former Chief Minister Amarinder's Singh presence in assembly sessions ever since Akalis came to power has been as rare as hen's teeth. Therefore, his presence for two consecutive days in the ongoing session was a pleasant surprise to many. His reinstatement as Chairman of Election Campaign Committee, seems to have worked well for him. Majority of Congress MLA showed support to him conspicuously.

New wheels
The top brass of the Punjab police is all set to get new pairs of wheels. A new Volkswagen Jeta has been ordered for DGP NPS Aulakh. It costs Rs 15 lakh. The Additional Director Generals of Police (ADGPs) would now move in Toyota Innovas. Ten of them have already been ordered.

A cup of tea please!
Officers in Punjab Civil Secretariat are given Rs 1000 per month as entertainment allowance for the office. This money is to be spent towards offering refreshments and sweet meats to the guests who visit them in their offices. However, as per rules, the claims for Rs 1000 are to be reimbursed only if the bills show tea, coffee or biscuits. If the officers order any other soft drink or lassi the claim can be rejected. So don't be surprised if on your visits to the Secretariat you are offered hot tea even if the weather is scalding hot outside.

No bending
Higher authorities in Punjab Police have introduced yoga exercises, bhangra classes to tuck in the bloating paunches of the officers. But the trouble seems to be swelling right under their noses. Security personnel employed at the Secretariat too seem to be suffering from inertia concomitant with bulging bellies. An example of this is their aversion to bend while frisking visitors at the rear entrance of the Secretariat. But the duty requires that every visitor be checked right down to his feet. To avoid the discomfort caused by bending, the security personnel have placed stools. Every visitor is made to stand on it and then checked. This saves the staff, the onerous task of bending down.

Where is he?
A game of cat and mouse was played between Congress and INLD leader Om Prakash Chautala during the recently held Monsoon session of the state assembly. Sensing Congress' plan to launch into diatribes against him in the case of his alleged disorderly behaviour with the Privilege committee headed by his bete-noire Karan Singh Dalal, Chautala was elusive most of the time. Finally the house was forced to adjourn the discussion on the privilege committee report till the next session, which most likely will not be held for another six months.

Heading: ‘Revive the art of letters, it bonds like no email can’ - Indian Express
Content:
The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum has directed Indiabulls Securities to refund Rs 10,000 and pay Rs 3,000 for causing mental agony to a complainant, after they allegedly demanded money from him, even after he had closed his account.

It has also been directed to pay Rs 1,100 as litigation costs. The complainant, Ranjit Singh Chandhoke, had taken a membership of Indiabulls Securities in April 2006, for which, he had deposited a cheque for Rs 10,000.

Singh said he received a call from the assistant relationship manager, a day later, telling him the cheque had been misplaced. He requested for another cheque of the same amount. He later requested the company not to trade on his behalf, as the amount of Rs 10,000 invested by him was reduced to Rs 7,319. He then requested for a refund and Rs 7,319 was refunded to him. The complainant alleged that, in January 2007, he found that even after closing his account, the company was still trading on his behalf.

Heading: CitiFinancial to pay up for deficiency in service - Indian Express
Content:
"The art of letters will come to an end before AD 2000. I shall survive as a curiosity," said Ezra Pound. Whether he was a clairvoyant who could predict the fate of the art of letter-writing is still to be contested, but his prophecy did come true.

No doubt the 21st century is the age of information boom: SMS, emails, social networking sites among others, but it has unfortunately, sounded a death knell for the much-loved art of yore: letter writing.

Gone are the days when lovers professed their undying love to each other through letters. Feelings are now expressed through SMS, using emoticons. The home-sick hosteller no longer writes home, he e-mails!

The coming of the internet and mobiles has shrunk the world, but at the same time, it has done away with the personal touch that was there in communication. I may sound old-fashioned, but I think the feeling of reading a letter, holding an inland in your hand is unbeatable.

Though it takes a fraction of a second to write an email, but the time used to pen a letter is actually time invested in some meaningful activity.

All of us have time constraints and so we want to do things in a jiffy. But in our quest to be fast, we have failed to see that technology has, despite bridging the distance between bodies, increased the distance between hearts. I still remember the days when I used to receive letters from my cousins, each syllable, the handwriting, captured my imagination.

People say that emails have made life easier; I feel they have made it dry. A sense of detachment prevails over the mails I receive from friends and relatives.

I still write letters to my friends, but the time constraint has engulfed me as well and I too, email. At the same time, however, I feel that the art of letters should be revived as it bonds people together like no email can.

Heading: SD College holds annual talent competition - Indian Express
Content:
The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum has directed CitiFinancial Consumer Finance to pay Rs 10,000 for deficiency in service.

The bank has also been asked to redraw the account of the complainant by taking the loan amount of Rs 6,800 as inclusive of interest with no bouncing charges to be recovered.

The complainant, Rajiv Kumar Bansal, had purchased an LG Television for Rs 7,600 in 2007 by paying Rs 1,000 as down payment and raising a loan for the remaining amount from Citi Financial Consumer Finance. The amount was to be paid in eight installments of Rs 850 each.

The complainant asserted that at the time of finance, he was told that the cheques would be presented on the 12th of every month as his salary was credited on the 10th of every month.

The company, however, presented the cheques on February 5, 2008 for which the complainant had to incur bouncing charges of Rs 393. Thereafter, he made the payment of the said cheque in cash to the representative of the bank who visited his house but after this the finance company again presented the cheque on February 12, 2008 and got the bouncing charges Rs 850 again.

The complainant averred that he was not aware of the bouncing charges of 12th February and deposited the amount of Rs 850 in the month of March, 2008 but due to negative balance for the month of February 2008, he again got the bouncing charges in March 2008. Furthermore, the complainant made the full and final payment with adjustment on March 23, 2008 and the executive got signed the affidavit and issued the receipt of full and final payment but despite this the cheques were not returned to him. The same were presented again on April 5, 2008 and May 6, 2008.

In its reply, CitiFinancial stated that the complainant had applied for and was granted a loan of Rs 10,200. The said loan was repayable in 12 equated monthly installments instead of eight as alleged in the complaint. They also denied that he was assured that the cheque would be presented on the 12th of every month.

The forum found that the original agreement between the parties in this respect was withheld by the bank and that was the primary document to suggest as to on which date the payment was to be made.

"An adverse inference is to be drawn against the finance company that they were to tender the cheque for payment on 12th of each month and not on 5th of the month, as they had been doing. The consequence thereof is that if the cheque is dishonoured, the bank is not entitled to any amount of Rs 225 as charged by them for bouncing charges of the cheque," the forum stated.

Heading: ‘Excessive use of Army not conducive for democracy’ - Indian Express

Heading: Punjab formulates new education scheme - Indian Express
Content:
The Army is being increasingly used to support Internal Security (IS) duties that include staging flag marches to restore confidence in the people as seen last in Gujarat following the blasts.

Now the focus has shifted to the Jammu region after controversy arose on the land earlier transferred to the Shri Amarnath Shrine Board. As many as 45 columns of the Army are presently employed in the region.

The Army is enforcing curfew, a responsibility of the police. They are expected to keep the 300-km long national highway to Srinagar open to ensure that the Kashmir valley is supplied and stocked with all the necessities of life. The flow of tourists and continued export of its fruit and other items to the mainland is also ensured by the Army.

Not very recently, in clear violation and defiance of Section 114 of the India Penal Code, which treats the imitation of army uniform as a cognizable offence, all the Central Police Organisations (CPOs) like the CRPF and BSF have started wearing similar uniforms, with minor and inconspicuous difference in shade and shoulder titles. The BSF has also started painting their vehicles green, akin to the Army. All this makes the Army virtually indistinguishable from the CPOs.

Now, the rioters do not know whether it is the CRPF or the BSF or the Army that they confront. This blurring identity has resulted in the Army losing its psychological advantage and the rioters have virtually lost "fear of the Army".

In a TV shot on August 7, Army vehicles were shown using red cloth as banners with the "INDIAN ARMY" written on it to impress their presence. What a travesty of imitating a 'stolen' identity.

Gen J J Singh as the Army Chief had written to the Home Ministry against the CPOs using the Army pattern of uniform but to no avail. Will the powers that be take notice and take corrective steps? There has also been a TV report of protesters being lathicharged by the Army.

If true, it was an extremely dangerous way of employing the Army.

Use of such methods will leave no difference between them and any police force and its 'shock and awe' value would stand nullified.

There was also a report of rioters pelting stones on Army convoys and the Army had to open fire in self-defence resulting in the death of a rioter. Perhaps, they misunderstood it to be a CPO or Para Military Forces' (PMF) convoy.

Never in the past have crowds attacked them in this manner and if intentional, the incident is most unfortunate and hints at things to come. An Army that loses respect of the people loses it value as their protectors and starts being viewed as their oppressor. The people might get alienated from such an Army.

Apart from being communal, the Jammu agitation for all practical purposes had high religious tones and connotations. Some rioters were seen carrying religious symbols and even the National Flag. Religion is a very sensitive and touchy affair. The need of firing by Army jawans on people carrying their religious symbols may put them in a dilemma.

One should not forget how some battalions of a particular community deserted their units in the aftermath of an attack on the Golden Temple during Operation Blue Star in 1984. Surely, we can avoid situations, which are not in conformity with our simple Jawans' religious sentiments.

The Jammu region has a large number of ex-servicemen reportedly taking part in the agitation, as evident from a general officer appearing on a news channel on August 8 and warning that even the ex-servicemen would be fired upon.

This may stretch the Jawans' loyalty between their present and former commanders and 'comrades in arms'.

One wonders why the CPOs and the PMF have not been fully used before using the Army. India has the biggest and largest CPOs and PMF in the whole world. Why have they not been used effectively? Why is the Army, a supposed 'last resort', being used as the first choice?

Excessive use of the Army is not conducive for democracy. To stop CPOs and PMF from using similar uniforms and vehicles, the Army must invoke Section 114 of the IPC and defaulters must be booked.

Heading: Have a query? Go to new cells of political parties - Indian Express
Content:
Free land, Rs 2.5 crore for private school

The Punjab government has formulated a new scheme to improve the poor state of education in the state.

Under this scheme, the state government will provide free land and Rs 2.5 crore as capital investment to open a new school that would be run and managed by the private sector.

Punjab Chief Secretary Ramesh Inder Singh said this while addressing an exposition on rural education revolution organised by the Kalgidhar Trust of Baru Sahib in Mohali late on Saturday evening.

The Chief Secretary, who was the chief guest at the exposition, said the scheme has evoked overwhelming response from leading industrial houses, willing to run and manage such schools in different parts of the state. "Our aim is to open at least one such school in every block every year," said Singh.

Lauding the services of the Kalgidhar Trust in the field of education, he urged the trust functionaries to link their academies and schools with the Edusat (education through satellite) programme of the state government.

Singh said the state government was planning to link all its senior secondary schools and colleges with the Edusat programme in the next five years.

"Our education system should be shaped in such a manner that instead of getting into the clerical jobs, the young generation can look forward to other innovative professions to meet the new challenges," said the Chief Secretary.

In his presidential address, Punjab Mandi Board Chairman Ajmer Singh Lakhowal said that due to the exorbitant fee structure, rural students could not afford to study in schools of the Kalgidhar Trust.

"The old education system was only capable of producing clerks, while the introduction of job-oriented courses has also failed to check unemployment," said Lakhowal, while complaining that the Punjab's farmers were not allowed to produce crops which reap more profits but were forced to produce such crops which yielded lesser profits.

"Due to this, the poor farmers are unable to impart quality education to their wards, most of whom are pushed into drug addiction, which has ruined the future of Punjab," Lakhowal said, while urging the Kalgidhar Trust to open at least 150 educational academies in rural areas of Punjab to impart quality education at a nominal fee structure.

Kalgidhar Trust spokesperson Iqbal Singh then announced that 150 educational academies and schools will be opened in the rural areas of Punjab. He also declared that a university to impart higher education in the state will be opened. At present, 32,000 students are being imparted moral-based education at 43 educational institutions of Kalgidhar Trust.

Former Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, Vice-Chancellor Dr Khem Singh proposed a vote of thanks.

Heading: MC polls: One-third women contestants, 6 of 15 ex-members in the fray - Indian Express
Content:
Looking for legal advice or thinking how to invest money, political parties in the city have a solution. The parties have various cells catering to voters with diverse backgrounds from various segments.

While colony cells for voters in slums and colonies have been known to have existed for long, new cells targetting the urban voters are being set up.

The Chandigarh Territorial Youth Congress has an 'Intellectual Cell'. It comprises professionals from various walks of life including doctors, engineers and bankers. The aim is to motivate the educated youth of the city to take active part in politics.

President of the cell Anurag Kohli says, "Politics is not a dirty word, it is the people who make it so. We wanted the message to be propagated among the youth of the city."

Since its inception, the members of the cell have held seminars at regular intervals for the youth. The cell propagates information among residents about using the Right to Information Act and also helps hem address basic problems like registering FIRs.

Other cells including Sports and Cultural Cell, Legal Cell and Doctor Cell are also in operation.

Similar is the case with the BJP that had launched an Investor Cell recently. Advice would be imparted to help people manage their investments.

The party spokesperson informed that the cells facilitate the parties in getting in touch with people from all segments.

The legal cell, which frequently takes up cases of those belonging to the poor section of the society, is one such example, added the spokesperson.

Heading: Six months after SC ruling, colleges yet to implement quota - Indian Express
Content:
Nearly one-third of the 69 contestants for the Kharar Municipal Council elections are women. Besides contesting from the five reserved wards, women candidates are also trying their luck from the general category wards.

Another surprising fact regarding this year's nominees is that only six of the total 15 members of the previous MC are in the fray this year. Only three former municipal councillors who ruled the house earlier are contesting the battle.

No former president of the MC, meanwhile, is in the fray. The main contest in most of the constituencies is between the ruling SAD-BJP combine and the Congress party.

The SAD-BJP combine, is fielding its candidates on the symbol of the 'Rising Sun', with support from Charanjit Singh, former MC president, also an independent MLA from Chamkaur Sahib. The 15 Congress candidates, meanwhile, are contesting on the party symbol of the 'Hand'.

The maximum number of candidates is from Ward No. 1 (11), while only two contestants are in fray at Ward No. 2.

Heading: New villages suffer MC apathy - Indian Express
Content:
Six months after the Supreme Court judgment giving instructions to start admissions under the Other Backward Class (OBC) category, none of the affiliate colleges of the Panjab University have started the same. With the Panjab University passing the buck to the Chandigarh Administration, the latter is still to come up with a decision.

The Supreme Court had announced for the implementation of the 27 per cent OBC quota in a phased manner from this year onwards. It had also asked the Panjab University to implement the same. Keeping this in mind, the varsity was to implement 7 per cent quota this year, followed by 7 per cent and 13 per cent respectively in the following two years .

The applications at the Panjab University, meanwhile, have been completed and the admissions will be held by September 15.

Bharam Parkash, president, OBC Forum, said: "When we contacted the Vice-Chancellor, he told us that the university has no discretion to ask colleges to implement the quota and it would be done by the Administration. We have received many queries and there are various students awaiting admission to different colleges of the PU."

The colleges had earlier been asked to submit information regarding their requirements about the staff and infrastructure, that would be needed to implement the quota.

Professor A C Vaid, principal, SD College, Sector 32, said: "Ideally it is the university that should be implementing the quota as the decision for the same was passed in the Syndicate meeting. The same body governs the affiliate colleges as well. Later we had submitted the details to the Administration, but the latter is silent on the issue and we have got no directions regarding the same."

With no answer having been received from the PU officials to the Administration, every one seems to be passing the buck. Raji P Srivastava, Director Higher Education said: "It is the education secretary who will decide about the issue as he is the Home and Social Secretary as well. We shall follow his directions."

Sanjay Kumar, education-cum-home secretary could not be contacted despite repeated attempts.

Heading: The guardian of time - Indian Express
Content:
Neither the bylaws nor any architectural norms apparently exist anymore in any of the villages

Even after city villages have been included in the Municipal limits of Chandigarh, the authorities are yet to accept these in the true spirit, as most villages lack basic amenities. Lack of concrete roads, streetlights, adequate health and sanitation services comprise a small list of the larger picture of neglect.

The facts stand substantiated in the Statistical Abstract released by the Chandigarh Administration earlier this week. The city villages cover an area of hundreds of acres, with each of 12 such villages covering nearly 600 to 700 acres of land on an average.

As the authorities appear least bothered in providing even basic facilities in these villages even after including them in the Municipal limits, the situation is deteriorating further.

As far as building bylaws are concerned, neither the bylaws nor any such architectural control norms apparently exist anymore in any of the villages. Be it haphazard construction or all kinds of architectural norms, all of it takes place in these villages. When asked, a senior MC official said, "We are still in the process of working out the modalities of framing certain policies for the villages".

When it comes to sanitation, filthy streets, overflowing sewerage pipelines with no proper drainage system and mosquitoes breeding on the streets and the village lanes are a common sight.

While the Administration and Municipal Corporation had recently framed proposals for the betterment of city villages, no major initiative has been implemented so far.

Heading: Rs 25-crore tax on cotton mills waived - Indian Express
Content:
If there were more than 24 hours in a day, Ashwani Koul would have still wanted more. A glance at his chock-a-block daily routine may leave an impression that the man needs to take a break once in a while. But Koul, the warden of Lajpat Rai Hall and Reader at the Biophysics department of the Panjab University, does not have time even to think about a break.

His day begins at five in the morning. "On weekends, I get up early to take part in the plantation and cleaning drives," he tells Newsline. He has recently been elected as the secretary of the PU Teachers' Association, adding more notes to his 'to-do' list.

From six to eight, he chalks out the day's plan, takes phone calls. And in between makes sure that his daughter is ready for school in time and that his wife, who works with a bank, reaches her workplace before 10. That done, he goes to the hostel for an hour.

"There are several things to be taken care of in the hostel at this hour. Location of rooms, file work, assigning leaves take a lot of time. This is also the time when students personally approach me with their urgent problems. Otherwise, I'm always available on the phone. The maintenance of the hostel is also taken care of," says Koul, who leaves for the department at 11 "unless there is a meeting with the DSW".

For lunch, he heads home but also makes it a point to check hostel food regularly. "I stop by the hostel during meal time to see if students have any complaint about food or other things. I even eat with them once in a while," says Koul.

By 2.30 pm, he is back to his department for practical classes. If he is free by 5, he meets the DSW or checks things at the hostel.

For about two hours from five in the evening, Koul spends time on his research work. A few minutes at home, and he is back at the hostel at half past seven. "I meet my students over a cup of tea. We have an informal session where they share notes about their studies, personal lives and other things. It's nice to interact with them at a personal level," he says.

Occasionally, he inspects the rooms also and then heads back home at 8.30 pm. After dinner with family, he goes to bed by 10 or 11 pm.

About his busy life, he says: "My mother used to say if you destroy time it destroys you. I don't want to be one."

Heading: Kaypee to move High Court, calls for Central observers - Indian Express
Content:
Narotam Dev Ratti and Madan Lal Bagga appointed Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the State Traders' Board, respectively

The Punjab government has decided to waive the Rs 25-crore tax arrear on cotton gimming mills.

Sources said a delegation of the mills' association had met Punjab Chief Minster Parkash Singh Badal in Bathinda some time back and gave a plea that in 2005, one per cent infrastructure tax was imposed on them, but they were unaware of it. They had urged that the old tax should waived, and they would make timely payments in future. Notably, there are 100 such mills in the state.

Today, after attending the function in which Narotam Dev Ratti and Madan Lal Bagga assumed office of Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Punjab State Traders' Board, respectively, Badal said, "These appointments were in keeping with the commitment made in the SAD-BJP's election manifesto to constitute State Traders' Board." He said the chairman and the vice-chairman have been given the status of cabinet ministers and they would act as a bridge between the bureaucracy and the traders.

Badal assured the trading community that all their genuine demands would be looked into.

Heading: City roads have claimed  100 lives this year, says study - Indian Express
Content:
Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee president Mohinder Singh Kaypee said his party would file a writ petition in the Punjab and Haryana High Court tomorrow against the "highhandedness" of Akalis in the coming Moga and Muktsar MC elections.

He alleged that the police of both the districts had neither allowed Congress candidates to file nominations nor let leaders secure party symbols.

"The Congress leaders have no option but to fight the September 14 elections as independents," Kaypee said.

He said, "We will move the court and seek a stay on elections and restart the entire process under the supervision of Central observers or at least the Army."

However, Moga MLA Joginder Pal Jain said, "Seeking legal remedy at this stage will not serve any purpose, as we have very little time on hand. The legal process takes time and atrocities of the Akalis are on the rise. We have videos to substantiate our claims. The police are illegally detaining our candidates and pressurising them to withdraw papers. The police are even slapping false cases of flesh trade against our women candidates. In this environment, who will fight elections?"

"Makhan Brar, son of former MLA Tota Singh, has his vote at three different places," he alleged.

"We have asked the candidates, who are ready to enter the fray, to fight as independents," Jain said.

Meanwhile in Muktsar, the Congress has decided to boycott election on all 23 seats. Vijay Sathi, a close confidant of Jagmeet Brar who is busy preparing for a rally tomorrow, said, "The aim of this rally is to tell the people that law and order machinery in Punjab has totally collapsed. It is a jungle raj and not democracy. Article 356 should be applied to Punjab."

Heading: Land case: Amarinder says he took leaf out of Badal’s book - Indian Express
Content:
The city roads have witnessed nearly 330 road accidents this year: killing 100 and injuring 300.

A recent study by the Chandigarh Traffic Police reveals that over 98 per cent of the accidents were due to human errors — over speeding and negligent driving.

In an accident at the Housing Board light point on August 31, the driver of a two-wheeler was killed after he rammed a truck. It was later found that he had jumped a red light, thus ramming into the truck.

Among the roads that spell danger, Dakshin Marg takes the lead, with 11 accidents having taken place on this stretch.

The Engineering department of the Chandigarh Administration has installed traffic lights on this road to manage the heavy rush of vehicles.

Madhya Marg, comes second with eight accidents on the stretch.

Traffic police officials claim that the traffic entering the city from the airport side is generally at a high speed, and is responsible for the high number of accidents.

All special drives undertaken by the traffic police like violation for speeding and drunken driving seems to be of no use as the numbers of road accidents is spiralling with each passing year.

The move by the traffic police officials to impart training to bus drivers and others a few months ago, too, received a lukewarm response, as very few drivers from Punjab and Haryana attended the same.

Heading: ‘BJP will scrap Article 370 in J&K if voted to power’ - Indian Express
Content:
Former Punjab chief minister Capt Amarinder Singh today turned the tables on CM Parkash Singh Badal by saying that the SAD-BJP government has also exempted land acquired by PUDA during the past one and a half years.

In a press statement issued today, he claimed that the government dropped land acquisition proceedings of some 302 acres in Nangalshama Chohak village on Hoshiarpur-Jalandhar road, 653 acres in Sultanwind in Amritsar, 201 acres in Barnala Kalan in Nawanshahr and 104 acres in Bullapur in Khanna.

The decision to exempt the land for private developers was based on the policy laid down by Badal during his previous tenure, when he exempted 87 acres for two projects, Amarjit Enclave and Dr's Enclave. The exemption of 32.5 acres was given under the same policy.

"My government had made Badal's policy more stringent by adding a rider that any such exemption to be given by PUDA must first get a no objection from the local Improvement Trust. The then Minister of Local Government Chaudhary Jagjit Singh and chairman of Amritsar Improvement Trust Jugal Kishore acted within the framework of the policy," claimed Amarinder.

He said the report was drafted by nine members of the House committee, out of which only three were from the Congress. He said, "There are seven cases pending in the Punjab and Haryana High Court about Veer Enclave project, including my case. This clearly makes the matter sub-judice, and ineligible for discussion in the House.

The Speaker has violated the rules of the Vidhan Sabha and also shown disrespect to the High Court. We will take a legal recourse."

Heading: Widow accuses cop of land grab - Indian Express
Content:
In charge of Punjab BJP affairs Balbir Punj today said if voted to power, the party would scrap Article 370.

He said they would also ask the Centre to clarify its stand on the statement given by Union Minister for Chemicals and Fertilisers and Steel Ram Vilas Paswan about according citizenship to Bangladeshis.

"Hindu families that migrated from Pakistan some 60 years ago and are living in Jammu and Kashmir have not yet been granted citizenship," he said. Punj said though the UPA government has won the vote of confidence, it lacks courage to face the Lok Sabha elections and these were likely to be postponed. Admitting to differences between the SAD and the BJP, Punj, however, said, "We are two different parties with different ideologies and styles of functioning."

"Out of the 13 LS seats, BJP will contest on three and SAD on 10," he said.

Heading: Board demands money to correct its own mistakes - Indian Express
Content:
A 75-year old widow, Sukhdev Kaur, of Rauli village in Moga has complained to the Vigilance Bureau, Ferozepur, that a Head Constable, who is a munshi with the Punjab Police, has been trying to usurp her property.

According to Sukhdev's complaint, her daughter-in-law Kamaljit Kaur, in connivance with the Head Constable and others, has been trying to usurp her husband's ancestral property worth crores of rupees by preparing forged will of her son.

He son, Sukhchain Singh, had died in September 2005. The complainant said Head Constable had got Sukhdev, her two married daughters, Paramjit Kaur and Charanjit Kaur, and some of their relatives booked in two criminal cases last year in March and June. In these cases, they were accused of cheating and hurting Kamaljit. Later in an inquiry conducted on the orders of DIG (Ferozepur Range), they were absolved of all charges.

However, using his clout, the Head Constable and Kamaljit got the FIRs reinstated. Sukhdev Kaur had also approached Punjab DGP NPS Aulakh, who marked the inquiry to Muktsar SP (Detective) Kuldeep Singh Dahel.

When contacted, Dahel said, "Everything will become clear after the inquiry."

She said in the complaint that in February this year, despite the court's orders, the Head Constable, with the help of Kamaljit, transferred 18 kanals in his son's name.

Sources in the VB said the Head Constable was facing several other charges and had allegedly amassed wealth through illegal means.

As per records, he had recently sold and bought properties worth Rs 50 lakh in his, his wife, and son's names.

Sources said he was also constructing a palatial house in Inder Singh Gill Nagar, a posh colony in Moga.

When contacted, Ferozepur SSP VB Sandeep Goel said, "We have shunted him out of the Vigilance Bureau on disciplinary grounds and sent him to his parent cadre, Punjab Armed Police (PAP), Jalandhar. I have received many complaints against him and am looking into the matter. If found guilty, he will be severely punished."

Heading: NRI woman sets up refuge for forced marriage victims - Indian Express
Content:
PSEB sends certificates with wrong names, 'demands' Rs 100 per correction

Fate of 33 students, who had appeared for class V examination of Punjab School Education Board (PSEB) last year in schools being run under the National Child Labour Project (NCLP), hangs in balance.

Certificates awarded to them by the board are full of errors. Their parents and school authorities alleged that the board has been demanding money to rectify the mistakes. Sources said the PSEB had demanded Rs 100 per mistake.

As the parents of students are barely able to make ends meet, many of them do small jobs to make a living. They said around 44 students had appeared in the class V exam last year, of which 10 failed.

However, a year later, when the board authorities sent their certificates, at least 33 had wrong names of the students, which led to resentment.

"Despite all odds, we had worked hard to qualify the exam and this is how they (the board) repay us," said Manga, a student. Neha, another student, echoed Manga's views.

"It is the duty of the PSEB to rectify these mistakes," said Sukhwinder Singh, District Education Officer (Primary). However, Dr Dalbir Singh Dhillon, Chairman, Punjab School Education Board, said the matter was in his notice.

"We have removed the board member who suggested that money should be taken to correct the mistakes. The errors will be rectified soon without charging a penny from the students," he said.

Heading: HIV positive couple has a harrowing time at PGI - Indian Express
Content:
An Indian-origin woman, who left her home to avoid being forced to marry a man chosen by her family in India, has founded a charity organisation to help women caught in similar situations. Birmingham-based Kelly Kaur was 16 when she left her house in Walsall.

Kaur, now a 39-year-old businesswoman, says, "I was in a situation where my parents tried to marry me off to a man from India. I always thought you could say no to an arranged marriage, but it turned out that I couldn't. I told the authorities, but they didn't want to get involved because it was a 'cultural thing'."

Kelly had to return home after her parents told the police that their daughter was under 16. Both parents are now dead, and Kelly is a happily-married mother of two. She has set up a new housing initiative called Thoroughcare Housing and Support to provide help to the victims of domestic violence and forced marriages.

It will also provide education and support to vulnerable adults and children seeking asylum. Kaur says, "I am not saying that arranged marriages don't work, but they should not be forced. We look to mediate with families and talk to them. I think that if someone could have sat down with my parents and explained it to them it could have been different. The British government has taken steps to prevent forced marriages that are often linked to the spate of honour killing, mainly in the Asian community."

Heading: 18-year-old killed by friends - Indian Express
Content:
An HIV positive couple, who came to the city from Saharanpur to get their infant daughter tested has been running from pillar to post for the last 15 days at the PGI. Alleging rude behaviour and apathy at the hands of the doctors and the PGI staff, the couple said they are having a harrowing time.

Father of four daughters, including the two-month old, Mukesh, a labourer, says doctors at the PGI turn their backs the moment they tell them they are HIV positive.

"They ask us to go to private doctors for the tests, I have no money left and do not know where to go," he said, adding they have been shoved away many times.

Their world shattered a year ago when both Mukesh and his wife were detected HIV positive. "I once took blood after I met with an accident. After we were detected positive, we got our first three daughters tested and fortunately all three of them are HIV negative," he said adding that they are currently taking treatment at the PGI for the past one year.

"We want to know the HIV status of our daughter. I wanted all my daughters to study, but due to paucity of money, I cannot afford their education too," he said.

A PGI spokesperson said she will inquire into the matter.

Heading: Nurmahal suicide: ‘Former SHO pressurising us’ - Indian Express
Content: Body of an 18-year-old boy, who was killed by his friends and buried in the fields, was recovered in Rahimpur village, near Kartarpur. The reason behind the youth's murder was said to be his alleged affair with the sister of one of his friends, Dharminder. Malkiat Singh had been missing since August 25, when he had gone with his four friends to attend a 'jagrata'. During investigations, when the police questioned his friends, one of them broke down and spilled the beans.

Heading: Drug courier killed in encounter - Indian Express
Content: In Nurmahal mass suicide case, kin of the deceased alleged in their application to the Jalandhar SSP that they were being pressurised to strike a compromise with the accused.  The suicides took place on June 7 last year, and the SHO was booked after a magisterial probe.  The complainants, Resham and Surjit Kaur, brother and sister of the deceased, Sukhdev, who committed suicide along with his pregnant wife and five-year-old daughter, alleged that the accused SHO has been sending people to threaten them. Notably, the court of Additional Sessions Judge had earlier dismissed the police plea, seeking cancellation of the case against former SHO Shiv Singh Kahlon.

Heading: ‘Everything in Chandigarh breathes of Le Corbusier’s art’ - Indian Express
Content:
An Indian drug courier was killed, while another was arrested in an encounter with BSF jawans this morning at Rajatal border outpost (BOP), near Attari land border. The BSF has recovered 4 kilograms of heroin and 13 cartridges from the accused. The slain courier has been identified as Soni, a resident of Chogawan village, while the arrested accused, Pratap Singh, is a resident of Chheharta.

The encounter took place when some Pak smugglers tossed a consignment of heroin towards the Indian side of the fence where these two couriers were waiting to receive it. On being stopped by the jawans, the drug smugglers on Pakistani side fired and the BSF retaliated. The Pakistani smugglers fled from the spot.

Heading: Cache of arms seized near border - Indian Express
Content:
"The City Beautiful is a living example of Le Corbusier's architectural acumen. Everything in the city breathes his art," exclaimed Professor Yoshiyuki Yamana, head of the Japanese delegation visiting the city to study Le Corbusier's work.

Japan is one of the participants in the project for Trans-border Nomination of Le Corbusier Urban and Architectural Work to UNESCO'S World Heritage List.

The delegation, which comprises five students apart from Professor Yamana, is on an eight-day visit to the city.

Talking to Newsline at the Government Art Museum and Gallery in Sector 10, Professor Yamana said the Museum of Western Art in Tokyo, built by Corbusier, is the same prototype of those built by him in Chandigarh and Ahmedabad. "Our area of research is the comparative study of the three museums. These buildings are categorised as modern heritage as we are putting them to use as well as trying to conserve them," he said.

Despite belonging to the same prototype, the buildings also have some variations which the delegation will be studying. "We are trying to know how the museum is being utilised and what restoration exercises can be undertaken in Tokyo to retain Corbusier's heritage. For instance, the reception and the undulatory windows of the museum in Tokyo were demolished a few years ago. We have, therefore, taken their detailed measurements so as to reconstruct them there," he said.

Styles such as hand grill, which are typical of Corbusier, have also fascinated the visiting students who will learn more about them. Juichi Iida, a final-year student of architecture said: "Corbusier was a contemporary architect and immensely talented. Apart from his artifacts, his open hand concept really interests me. I plan to do my post-graduation from the city for I would like to know more about his work." Juichi has written his thesis on the open-hand concept. "After visiting the city, I have come to know that the city has truly realised this concept," smiles Juichi.

Other than Corbusier, it is the Indian food that has the Japanese hooked. "The spices and the aroma of Punjabi cuisine are completely irresistible. We have been relishing the food everyday," says Okawa Hirushi, another student.

Professor Kiran Joshi of Chitkara School of Planning and Architecture says students from the college too will go for an exchange programme to Tokyo to study Corbusier's work. "Our students will acquire more knowledge about the legend and his work in Japan through the exchange."

Heading: Risky Business - Indian Express
Content:
In the year's first-ever seizure of arms' cache on the Indo-Pak border, 8 Battalion of the Border Security Force (BSF) seized three AK-47 assault rifles, eight pistols and seven latest timer devices, used in improvised explosive devices (IEDs), in the wee hours today near Kalas border outpost in Amarkot, Tarn Taran.

The cache also included eight magazines of AK-47 and 731 ammunitions of AK series of rifles, besides 16 magazines of pistols and 362 rounds.

While seizures of heroin along the border have been taking place in the past regularly, the arms' cache recovery was first since September 2007 last year, when weapons were seized at Ratto Ke in Khemkaran sector. "At that time, we had recovered two AK-47 rifles, a Pakistan-made MP3 rifle and six pistols," BSF DIG (Intelligence), Punjab Frontier, Jagir Singh Saran told The Indian Express.

Saran said Pakistan-based terrorist outfits had stepped up their activities after the February 2008 general elections. "Pakistan may or may not be involved, but terrorist outfits based there are definitely behind this," asserted Saran.

Out of the seven timer devices seized, three could have been programmed to trigger a device for as long as a period of six months, sources said.

Sources said the AK-47 assault rifles seized today were made in China and an analysis of markings on the pistols and metallurgical properties revealed that they were made in Pakistan, most likely in Baluchistan.

After an exchange of fire at 3.20 am, the intruders on the Pakistani side ran away leaving a gunny bag full of weapons near the boundary line.

Heading: ‘I’m  not like Prerna’ - Indian Express
Content:
cumentary maker Ajay Bhardwaj holds his interactions with reality

Does he make any money out of it? There is of course this huge intellectual satisfaction, but can passion rule over paisa? Is this soul satisfaction enough for survival? While questions play musical chairs in our head, Ajay Bhardwaj pushes the stop button and lays out his own dilemmas. "I confront them all the time, this constant questioning, but I choose to hold interactions with reality and I am aware of the very small space I work in...so, I know that this is only as far as I can go," documentary-maker and an ex TV guy, Bhardwaj has learnt the fine art of survival, and makes the points for it. "Take Ek Minute Ka Maun. Before JNU student Chandrasekhar Prasad was killed in 1997 in Sivan, I was just another mainstream television producer churning out programmes like Turning Point, game shows, chat shows. It was this one incident that made me gather footage and zoom on reality, and before we knew, it spiralled into a mass student movement," eleven years and Ajay's documentary is still running strong. Justice has been delayed, but Ajay has made his point. "The film gave immense power to students, it became a source of inspiration for them. It was another roar after Mandal." The trajectory on reflecting on things beyond the call of duty was always there, in this instance, it took a turn for good. "I've never gone back to television ever since for it's not the same. It has lost its strength of features," says Ajay, dealing with a different reality. "Not the reality of telly today, this one's a risky business." He's dealt with the pangs of Partition, the bond between Dalits and sufism, the plight of farmers and agriculture, and most of his works have been upfrontly agitational and outrightly political. "But luckily, I was never pulled into a controversy," he smiles. "There are forces at work which tamper with the themes chosen, but I am not the one who can be silenced. At least I'd like to believe so." It's this focus that compels Ajay to refuse to give legitimacy to the Censor Board by acknowledging their existence. "I am part of those documentary makers who bypass the Board, and hence, are never part of the National awards," he reflects.

The process of documentary making is self learning. "You tell a story to yourself first and then to the audience, and the amount of discovery made is immense for it gives the maker a possibility of contemplation and communication," feels Ajay, whose documentaries on his land, Punjab, border on the same thought - quest. Is there a future for documentaries, we probe, looking for growth and acceptance. "Technology has pushed it quite a few notches high. Even the tech illiterates are picking up digital cameras and recording realities we never get to see on the telly. The form has opened up tremendously," Ajay's quite positive.

Cameras have turned on oneself, and it's a time for personal narratives. Still, Ajay feels it's not enough. "Issues are mounting and thousands won't work in the vastness of this country...we need more." The room is always big enough for improvement.

Heading: Take the Fall - Indian Express
Content:
Theatre's 'Khoobsurat Bahu', television's much-loved bahu and mom, a divorce amidst controversies and now a judge on a reality show, Shweta Tiwari is not the one to look back. Life moves on and in her case, it moves ahead. Many cried as she cried on Kasuatii Zindagi Kay, then the Nach Baliye stint with ex-husband Raja, who left her on turbulent grounds, and now she is winning hearts again, as the judge of Aaja Mahi Vay (on Star Plus). In town to promote the reality dance show, Tiwari tells that judging is a "tough job. When I was a participant I wondered why I was unable to perform. Though I don't approve of all the judges, now I know what it is to be in that chair."

And before we could question her qualifications as a judge, she shoots," I have never lost a dance contest in school or college. For the show I read books, watched serials, I have done my homework, you see! When I say something is right or wrong while judging, I know what I'm talking about." So how's the new look after Prerna? "That was not Prerna, the straight hair look is Shweta Tiwari look. There was no image setting for the role." About the controversies regarding co-judge Ronit Roy she says, "He is the best to work with because he is very professional. After Kasautii, we are together judging and it's great working with him. Differences of opinion are bound to occur but that's that." As for the future she has no plans, "All I want is to become a versatile actor," she smiles.

Fame, tells Shweta, has not changed her, neither has divorce. "My daughter Palak is my life. I don't want to react on things related to Raja because we are two different individuals. It was a bad phase that's over now. I'm looking towards the future now." The show, ironically promises a marriage to the winner couple. "Marriage is not an agreement but a promise. If a dance competition breaks your relationship, then it wasn't worth it to begin with," Tiwari has the last word.

Let's Dance
Aaja Mahi Vay's dance couples Manika and Manit, Jashan and Tahira (the couple from Chandigarh) are all excited about the show and the city where they performed at Moti Ram Arya School. While host Vineet Singh is focussing only on his singing.

Heading: Sing On! - Indian Express
Content:
Here's a peek at the fall-winter trends you need to keep in mind this season

Colours

Think earthy this autumn. When Rohit Bal launched his autumn-winter line at the last fashion week, the ramp came alive in metallic hues. Bal's ashtadhatu collection, with its quilted jackets, shifts and silk jersey dresses, played up copper, gold and silver with a few beiges, browns and plums thrown in. Likewise, Anamika Khanna too showcased deep chocolates, charcoals and greys, while Ashish Soni enlivened his palette with a hint of bright blue, and magenta and red as sashes and belts. Think blue, think olive as well as deep jewel tones like mauve and purple. It's also the season for monotones, so give the prints a miss.

Silhouette

You might as well hit the gym while there's still time, because this season the silhouette is all about keeping it close to the body. Herve Leger's famous bandage dress makes a comeback with designers like Ranna Gill and Bal making their own versions. Newbie designer Prashant Verma, makes it a metaphor for a wound, because as he claims, the "youth represents all that is best and worst in the generation." Go for severe constructs like structured jackets in jacquards and sheath dresses. Slim fit pants, cigarette trousers and skinny jeans are the order of the day.

Indigenous

Influences

Wear your patriotism on your sleeves and pay your tribute to incredible India. Go for desi handicrafts that are bound to give your ensemble a remarkable facelift. While designer Nitin Bal Chauhan has infused the rich tribal folk traditions of his native town Chamba on to an otherwise Gothic collection, Atsu Sekhose brings to the fore his Naga sensibilities by giving his western clothes an Asian sensibility and using fabrics like handloom. Brothers Shantanu and Nikhil Mehra have used appliqué work of heritage Indian jewellery motifs besides handmade kaantha techniques. "Increasingly, Indians are becoming global citizens and people always like to show a bit of their roots wherever they are. That's why we have focused on it in our collection," says Nikhil.

Accessories

If you think the severity of your ensembles might cramp your style, jazz up the accents. Go for high-gloss crocodile skin, suede and patent leather bags. This season semi-precious stones like lapis lazuli and porphyry are the latest hits. Fendi's autumn-winter collection sees a return to the classic handback silhouette — semi-rigid and structured. As for shoes, start practising the catwalk. Tottering heels or ankle boots in suede or patent leather are the order of the day. 

So get started and stock up your wardrobe. The season's set to begin.

Heading: In the groove - Indian Express
Content:
While talent shows crowd TV schedules, BIG 92.7 FM brings singing competition 'Koyel Punjab Di' to the city. Organized in association with Dabur Vatika India Limited, "The contest will seek to identify new singers from Punjab," Siddharth Bhardwaj, Regional Director, North 1, BIG 92.7 FM, tells us, adding that a road shows was organsied before the event in city colleges including MCM DAV College, GCG-11, GC-42 and GC-46. "Around 60 singers have already been selected from these institutions and the final 'Koyel Chandigarh' will be held at DT malls, IT Park," he says that the contest is being held across five cities- Ludhiana, Chandigarh, Amritsar, Patiala and Jalandhar.

"The contest is open only for girls of Punjab and the five finalists from these five cities will come together for the grand finale that will be held in Chandigarh on September 28. The winner will get a once-in-a-lifetime chance to become the on-air singing sensation on Big 92.7FM," says Adarsh Sharma, Sales Head (Northern Region), Dabur India Ltd.

Heading: Rock Da Party! - Indian Express
Content: Unwind and be who you really are' that was the call and Bacardi Night Shift lived up to. Chandigarh's social enthusiasts had a free-spirited experience, at 'a night of musical extravaganza' on Saturday Night at Peninsula, Panchkula. Bacardi presented the first ever Bacardi Night Shift party of the season.The place saw a crowd of 150-200 youngsters dancing to the groovy tracks of DJ Megha. With "Bollywood" as the theme of the party, a similar experience was created for the guests where the venue looked just right.The experience was created with a whole new cocktail menu incorporating Bacardi cocktails, brilliant house and electronic music and water games. The guest list included the expatriate community who added to the excitement of the evening. It was surely an evening to remember!

Heading: More NRIs head home now to ‘save their skin’ - Indian Express
Content:
Two parties rocked the tricity. Here's what happened

Groovy. If we have to sum up Saturday night party at Ozone Fitness 'n' Spa in Sector 9, then groovy is your word. After all, it's not everyday that a fitness centre allows its members to kick the keds and strap up stilletoes. As part of their annual big bash - cocktail and dance - folks at Ozone threw the party of the year - liquor in full free flow, hot sumptuous snacks doing the rounds and members dancing till the wee hours of the morning to none other than Siingh is King. Believe me, the song rocks! And it was also one of those rocking Page 3 fares where people behaved themselves and no scuffle was reported. "It's our way of maintaining relations and bonding with the members," quips the GM, Vikram Kapoor. Well, the party sure was a hit.

Meanwhile, at the risk of sounding a tad critical, Chandigarh guys really need to straighten up their act - dress and drink-wise. While the ladies (most of them - thank god for Sex and the City!) experimented with their look on Saturday, boys and men walked in wearing everything but Saturday Night Fever. So we had Himesh Reshammiya caps (seriously, you wear it only to golf), bad Tees, faded jeans suffering from gravitational pull, sneakers and flowery shirts! As for the girls, while the exception for salwar kameez and sarees is always there, please play with your hair. And fitted doesn't mean breathlessly skin tight, always carry a clutch to a party, flowing floral skirts are for Sunday brunch, choose patent leather peep-toes over strappy sandals, and the last but not the least, avoid wearing noodle strap ganjis! That's all folks!

Heading: Moved by widow’s plight, councillor builds house for her in Panchkula village - Indian Express
Content:
Cost-effective skincare, treatments have many foreigners queuing up

With more and more people visiting India from all over the world for their medical requirements, health tourism is fast catching up in the country. Chandigarh is not far behind either, though not many of the patients coming here from abroad are tourists; they are non-resident Indians with roots in the region.

And while the most common treatments offered in India are heart surgery, knee transplant and dental care, Chandigarh sees most patients making a beeline for skin clinics.

On his visit to India this time, UK resident Dileep Shukla wants to consult a dermatologist for his wife who requires sittings for laser therapy to get rid of facial hair and pigmentation. After exploring all possibilities in the UK, the Shuklas decided to avail of the latest technology here at nearly one-tenth of the cost.

"Certainly, the cost of treatment offered here is the biggest attraction for NRIs like us. And the fact that Indian expertise now is at par with the best in the world, it makes all the sense to come here and save money. I have explored the services available in the UK and found that India offers the same treatment at very cheap rates," reasons Shukla, a pharmacist who visits India twice a year.

And the Shuklas aren't alone who have chosen Chandigarh for cosmetic and dermatological treatments. The numbers of NRIs coming here for facelift, botox, hirsuitism (facial hair) and treatment for pigmentation is increasing by the day.

Claiming to have treated nearly 500 NRIs in 2007 alone at his hospital, Dr Vikas Sharma of the National Skin Hospital says the treatments ranging from anti-wrinkle facelifts, botox, hirsuitism and other expensive laser treatments are quite a rage with the patients from overseas.

"There is a vast difference in the rates of the treatments offered in the West and that in India. In most cases, the same treatments offered in countries like the US or the UK cost 10 to 20 times more than what is being charged here," says Dr Sharma.

He has a patient couple coming from the US after regular intervals for treatment of pigmentation. Dr Sharma says while a single sitting in anti-ageing treatment, involving blastoplasty, costs Rs 2,000 in India on an average, it is available for Rs 50,000 in the US or the UK.

Pigmentation removal procedures available here at Rs 1,500 per sitting cost around Rs 40,000 per sitting in the western countries.

The Fortis Hospital in Mohali, too, has many foreign patients lining up for the cost-effective skin and laser treatment. Dr Daljeet Kaur, head of the dermatology department, says the patients were being offered special packages to make their stay comfortable.

"Since laser and dermatology treatments are not covered in the insurance policies, these treatments get more expensive in the western countries. With all latest technologies now available in India, the difference in the cost is a major attraction for the foreigners,"

she says.

"We are getting a lot of queries for treatments like botox and facelifts. It makes a lot of economic sense for the patients to come here for botox treatment, which takes just half an hour and costs Rs 350 per unit. In the US, it costs at least $100 per unit," says Dr Kaur. She adds that the packages offered by the hospital club the treatment cost and the stay in the city.

Heading: Police claim to crack ‘contract killing’, 3 held - Indian Express
Content:
The municipal councillor of Sector 12, Panchkula, is all set to do something that hardly any of her predecessors or colleagues has ever done. Moved by the plight of a 76-year-old widow in her ward, Lilly Bawa is building a home for her, spending money from her own pocket.

After her son and daughter-in-law died a few years ago, Prakasho, a resident of Railla village, was left with just a pension of Rs 100 in the name of a monthly income and two minor grandchildren — Dharmo and Deepi — to support. While Dharmo is 15 years old now, Deepi is a year younger.

"I have been in touch with the poor old lady for a long time now and always wanted to help her. Prakasho had three sons. While one of them died, the other two left her long ago to fend for herself. With hardly any source of income, Prakasho is raising two of her grandchildren. Villagers offer them some food every day," said Lilly Bawa.

She said the old woman had no place to stay and was putting up in a small, dingy room in a corner of the village.

Bawa said ever since she got to know of the condition of Prakasho, she had wanted to do something for her. "As it was for the first time that I contested and got elected, I tried to do something for her in my capacity as a councillor. I talked to Municipal Council officials about her plight, but there was no provision under which the lady could be helped. I then decided to help Prakasho on my own," said Bawa.

A proper house is now being constructed to replace the dingy room where the three were staying. "The cost is currently estimated at Rs 35,000, which may later increase. The work is in full swing and we expect the house to be ready in a month's time," said Bawa.

This is not the first time that Bawa has done such social work. She sponsors the education of a poor girl and two boys of her ward.

As for Prakasho, she is simply overwhelmed and overjoyed. She can be seen busy assisting the labourers who are constructing her house. "It has come as a pleasant surprise for an old woman like me. I never expected to have a house of my own. Bawa has proved that there are still some noble people in this world," she said.

After the house, Bawa said, she planned to help the family of three increase its earnings.

Heading: 4 days to go, poll scene hots up - Indian Express
Content:
Deceased's 'missing' wife booked, her 'lover' arrested

The Kharar police claimed to have cracked an eight-month-old murder case by registering a case against the deceased's wife, her "lover" and her daughter, and arresting three persons, including a contract killer.

The accused had allegedly thrown the body of Amrik Singh, aged around 40 years and a resident of Bhagomajra village near Kharar, into a canal after killing him. Amrik's wife, her daughter and another accused are reportedly still

at large.

The police said Amrik's brother-in-law Gurmeet Singh had lodged a missing report with the police on January 29 after his wife Harwinder Kaur alias Binder reportedly told him that Amrik had left the house after a spat with her on January 27 and did not return.

The police claimed that Gurmeet recently came to them after a local resident told him that one Balbir Singh alias Beera of Bagwali village had an affair with Binder who wanted to "eliminate" her husband as he had allegedly forced her into "prostitution".

According to the police, Binder reportedly met Beera on January 25 and sought his help to kill Amrik. In return, she allegedly offered money and promised to marry him, the police said.

Officers said Binder and Beera hired Naib Singh of Bagwali village to kill Amrik and gave him Rs 50,000 for the job.

Naib, his friend Sandeep Singh, Binder, Beera and another person gathered at Amrik's house on January 26 and after making him drink excessive liquor strangulated him to death, using a dupatta, said the police.

Amrik's body was dumped in the Bhakra canal near Morinda on the night of January 27, claimed the police.

While Beera and two others have been arrested, the rest are absconding.

According to the police, the only fault of Amrik's teenaged daughter, who was named as an accused in the FIR, was that she was witness to the crime and did not report it to the police.

Heading: Pak players to train at CLTA - Indian Express
Content:
PU STUDENTs' ELECTIONS: Amid indecisions, chaos and confusion, parties spend Sunday trying to reach out to maximum voters, finalising strategies

With the students' elections in Panjab University just a few days away, student bodies are busy utilising every single moment. Taking no chances, each party is ready with its poll strategy and is trying to reach out to the maximum voters possible.

The parties spent the Sunday afternoon campaigning in the girls' hostels while the evening was reserved for the boys' hostels. This year's elections are set to be different from the previous ones, with the Lyngdoh Committee recommendations in force.

Newsline takes a look at what is going on in the campus.

SOI takes a u-turn
When Newsline had reported earlier that the Students' Organisation of India (SOI) was going to form an alliance with the Indian National Students' Organisation (INSO), the former had refuted the report and declared Parambir Singh Sunny as its presidential candidate. On Sunday, however, the INSO declared its panel with Sukshdev Kundu, senior research fellow with the UGC Environment Science, as its presidential candidate and Parambir Singh Sunny of UILS as the general secretary.

Parties reach out to girls
The parties campaigned hard at the girls' hostels on Sunday, motivating them to vote for them. Talking to Newsline, SOPU president Barinder Dhillion said: "The votes of girls are definitely important. We are personally reaching out to all girls on the campus and we promise them support of every kind." Most of the parties, however, do not have any girl campaigning for them.

Confusion over alliance
After SOI, which declined an alliance first and then accepted one with the INSO, it was the NSUI that exhibited indecision. It remained busy deciding the alliance till Saturday and finally went ahead with SOPU. Members of the NSUI kept holding meetings with both SOPU and PUSU leaders till late evening and finally decided to truck with SOPU. The party took a long time to reach a consensus as the members remained divided on the alliance. Half of them wanted to forge an alliance with SOPU while the rest wanted to go with PUSU. The NSUI knew too well that it was a very weak party to contest independently and had to form an alliance.

Panels not decided yet
The student unions contesting the polls are yet to decide their panels, courtesy the Lyngdoh Committee's recommendations. With the committee barring leaders with criminal cases registered against them from contesting the polls, the parties are finding it difficult to get candidates. While many of the old candidates cannot contest now, not many new students are willing to jump in the fray. The parties are to submit the panels by Monday.

Heading: Rajat, Manav enter second round - Indian Express
Content:
In the ongoing inter-house football tournament at Guru Nanak Public School, Sarabha Nagar, Ludhiana, Shaheed Bhagat Singh house defeated Prof Mohan Singh House in the final by 3-0. All the goals were scored in the first half through Harjot Singh (2 goals) and Jaskaran Singh (1 goal).

After the First Half, the team of Prof. Mohan Singh House was a changed team and played with better coordination and understanding. Heading: Gayatri clinches Under-13 title - Indian Express
Content:

In a keenly fought match, both potted the red ball early. The first frame it was almost neck to neck, when Rajat came with a good break and won the first frame. In the second frame, Sandeep came with a nice break of 35 to grab the frame. In the deciding frame, Rajat made good break of 38 to clear the frame to win the game 2-1.

In another close contest, Manav Dhawan outplayed Sanjay Duggal 2-1(69-100, 100-52, 100-82). On the other hand, it was a one-sided encounter between Ashu Duggal and Amit Verma in which the latter prevailed over his opponent 2-0, (100-73, 100-78).

In the junior section, Ankit Sharma emerged too good for Madhur Mukhi after he cleaned up him at 2-0 (50-31, 50-23). It was an easy outing for Ankit Sharma.

In nail biting snooker event, Arif Akhtar of Indian Oil Corporation Ltd., outclassed Mandeep Makkar 3-2, (61-49, 67-26, 67-24, 59-42, 53-22). Top seed Rajat Khaneja in senior snooker event, beat Vijay Bhopali 3-0, (49-13, 54-26, 79-25) to move ahead. All eyes will be on Rajat on Monday to see him play in the second round.
